title: How do you implement rollback in a Saga pattern using orchestration?
shortTitle: How to implement rollback in a Saga using orchestration

s1_definition.profdef: Rollback in an orchestrated Saga is not a database rollback but a sequence of compensating transactions executed by the central orchestrator when a forward step fails. The orchestrator tracks the Saga's state as it completes each local transaction, and on failure it invokes, in reverse order, a compensating transaction for every step that already committed — a refund for a charge, a release for a reservation, a cancel for an order — each of which semantically undoes its forward step. These compensations must be idempotent and retryable so the orchestrator can safely re-run them, and the Saga ends in a consistent terminal state of either fully completed or fully compensated.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India processing Rajesh's order with a case manager (the orchestrator) holding a checklist. The manager ticks off each completed step: order created, stock reserved, money charged. If a later step fails, the manager does not have a magic undo button; instead the manager walks back down the checklist in reverse, doing the opposite action for each ticked item — refund the money, release the stock, cancel the order. Because a courier might get lost, the manager is careful that doing "refund" twice is harmless, so repeating a correction never causes a double refund. At the end, either the whole order went through or it was cleanly unwound.
s1_definition.oneliner: Saga rollback is the orchestrator running idempotent compensating transactions in reverse for every step that already committed, because there is no shared database rollback across services.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rollback in an orchestrated Saga is not a database rollback but a sequence of compensating transactions executed by the central orchestrator when a forward step fails. The orchestrator tracks the Saga's state as it completes each local transaction, and on failure it invokes, in reverse order, a compensating transaction for every step that already committed — a refund for a charge, a release for a reservation, a cancel for an order — each of which semantically undoes its forward step. These compensations must be idempotent and retryable so the orchestrator can safely re-run them, and the Saga ends in a consistent terminal state of either fully completed or fully compensated.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India processing Rajesh's order with a case manager (the orchestrator) holding a checklist. The manager ticks off each completed step: order created, stock reserved, money charged. If a later step fails, the manager does not have a magic undo button; instead the manager walks back down the checklist in reverse, doing the opposite action for each ticked item — refund the money, release the stock, cancel the order. Because a courier might get lost, the manager is careful that doing "refund" twice is harmless, so repeating a correction never causes a double refund. At the end, either the whole order went through or it was cleanly unwound.

**One line to remember:** Saga rollback is the orchestrator running idempotent compensating transactions in reverse for every step that already committed, because there is no shared database rollback across services.

sections.s2_technical:
The first thing to be clear about is that Saga rollback is semantic compensation, not transactional rollback. Each forward step already committed its own local database transaction in its own service, so those commits are permanent and cannot be undone by a database ROLLBACK. To reverse a committed step you run a compensating transaction that performs the inverse business action: you do not delete a payment row, you issue a refund; you do not un-commit a reservation, you release it; you do not erase an order, you set it to cancelled. Compensation is a new forward action that semantically negates a previous one.

In orchestration, the orchestrator owns this. It defines the ordered forward steps T1, T2, T3 and, for each step that needs undoing, a corresponding compensation C1, C2, C3. As it executes, it records the Saga's progress in durable state — after T1 it records that C1 is now owed, after T2 that C2 is owed, and so on — so that even across a crash it knows exactly which compensations are required. When a step, say T3, fails, the orchestrator stops going forward and runs the compensations for the steps that already succeeded, in reverse order: C2 then C1. Reverse order matters because later steps often depend on earlier ones, so you unwind in the opposite sequence to how you built up.

Several properties make this robust. Compensations must be idempotent, because the orchestrator may retry a compensation after a transient failure, and refunding twice or releasing stock twice must have the same effect as doing it once, usually enforced with an idempotency key per compensation. Compensations must be retryable and should themselves be durable actions, because a compensation can fail too, and the orchestrator must keep retrying until it succeeds, often with backoff, and alert for manual intervention if it cannot. The orchestrator persists the Saga state, so after a crash it resumes and completes any pending compensations rather than leaving a half-unwound flow. And you must respect non-compensatable steps: some actions cannot be undone, like sending a physical shipment, so you order them last or treat them as pivot points after which the Saga can only go forward, never back.

Concretely, when payment fails in an order Saga, the orchestrator, having recorded that order creation and stock reservation already committed, runs release-stock then cancel-order, each idempotent, and marks the Saga CANCELLED. If instead the Saga had already charged payment and a later step failed, the compensation for the payment would be a refund. The orchestrator is the single place that knows the compensation set and the order, which is exactly why orchestration makes rollback clean compared to choreography, where the compensation logic would be scattered.

A senior engineer adds the production mechanics. Use a workflow engine such as Temporal, Camunda, or Spring State Machine, which provides durable Saga state, automatic retries, timeouts, and visibility, so you do not hand-roll the state persistence and retry loops. Pair each forward step with the transactional outbox so the step and its event are atomic, and make each compensation a first-class operation exposed by the owning service. Keep the orchestrator focused on coordination and state, not business rules, to avoid a god-orchestrator. The result is that rollback becomes a well-defined, observable, recoverable process: for any failed Saga, the orchestrator drives the exact reverse compensations to a consistent end, and you can see at any moment which compensations ran and which are pending.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India runs an order Saga — reserve stock, charge payment, schedule shipment — and a step can fail after earlier steps have committed and even after money has been charged.

Problem 1 — If shipment scheduling fails after payment was already charged, a database rollback cannot recover the money, because the charge committed in the payment service's own database. The orchestrator must issue a refund — a compensating transaction — to undo the charge.

Problem 2 — Compensations must run in reverse order and be idempotent. The orchestrator records which steps committed, then on failure runs refund payment, then release stock, then cancel order, in that reverse sequence, and each compensation is safe to retry so a lost acknowledgement never causes a double refund.

Problem 3 — A compensation itself can fail transiently, so the orchestrator retries it with a bounded number of attempts and keeps the Saga state durable so it can resume after a crash.

What the code will do: a runnable demo implements `OrderSagaOrchestrator` that executes reserve-stock, charge-payment, schedule-shipment, recording the compensations owed after each committed step. Shipment is forced to fail, so the orchestrator rolls back by running the recorded compensations in reverse — refund, release, cancel — using idempotent compensation methods, and retries a compensation that fails once to show retryability. The Saga ends CANCELLED with money refunded and stock released.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: order ORD-900 for Rajesh (SAV2001), 2 units of BOOK-1 at Rs.50000, with shipment forced to fail after payment is charged.

Step 1: The orchestrator runs T1, reserving 2 units of stock, and records that it now owes a RELEASE_STOCK compensation.

Step 2: The orchestrator runs T2, charging Rs.50000, and records that it owes a REFUND_PAYMENT compensation. It also records a CANCEL_ORDER compensation.

Step 3: The orchestrator runs T3, scheduling shipment, which fails because no courier is available and throws. Money has already been charged, so a database rollback cannot help.

Step 4: The orchestrator sets the Saga state to COMPENSATING and begins rollback, popping compensations in reverse order (last recorded first). The first popped is CANCEL_ORDER.

Step 5: The CANCEL_ORDER compensation fails once with a transient error, so the orchestrator retries it, and on the second attempt it succeeds — demonstrating retryable compensations.

Step 6: The orchestrator pops REFUND_PAYMENT and issues the refund of Rs.50000, which is idempotent so a repeat would be harmless. Then it pops RELEASE_STOCK and releases the 2 units, also idempotent.

Step 7: With all compensations done, the orchestrator marks the Saga CANCELLED. The end state is consistent: shipment never happened, money refunded, stock released, order cancelled — a clean rollback with no shared transaction.

Final output:

```
18:00:00 INFO    [INVENTORY] reserved 2 for ORD-900
18:00:00 INFO    [PAYMENT] charged ORD-900 Rs.50000
18:00:00 SEVERE  [SHIPMENT] FAILED to schedule ORD-900
18:00:00 SEVERE  [SAGA] forward step failed → ROLLBACK via compensations in reverse order
18:00:00 WARNING [ORDER] cancel transient failure (will retry)
18:00:00 WARNING [SAGA] compensation CANCEL_ORDER attempt 1 failed, retrying
18:00:00 WARNING [ORDER] COMPENSATE cancelled ORD-900 (attempt 2)
18:00:00 WARNING [PAYMENT] COMPENSATE refunded ORD-900 Rs.50000
18:00:00 WARNING [INVENTORY] COMPENSATE released 2 for ORD-900
18:00:00 WARNING [SAGA] ORD-900 CANCELLED (money refunded, stock released)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  run(ORD-900, Rs.50000)
    │
    ▼ forward (record compensation owed after each commit)
  T1 reserve stock  ──▶ push C: RELEASE_STOCK
  T2 charge payment ──▶ push C: REFUND_PAYMENT
                    ──▶ push C: CANCEL_ORDER
  T3 schedule shipment ──╳ FAIL (money already charged → no DB rollback)
    │
    ▼ ROLLBACK (pop LIFO = reverse order, each idempotent + retried)

  pop REFUND_PAYMENT → refund Rs.50000 (idempotent)
  pop RELEASE_STOCK  → release 2 units (idempotent)
    │
    ▼
  state = CANCELLED  (consistent: no shipment, refunded, released)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Rollback in an orchestrated Saga is not a database rollback, and getting that distinction right is the heart of the answer. Each forward step has already committed its own local transaction in its own service, so those commits are permanent and cannot be reversed with a database ROLLBACK. To undo a committed step I run a compensating transaction that performs the inverse business action — a refund to undo a charge, a release to undo a reservation, a cancel to undo an order — so compensation is a new forward action that semantically negates a previous one, not a technical rollback.

In orchestration the orchestrator owns this entirely. It defines the ordered forward steps and, for each step that needs undoing, a corresponding compensation, and as it executes it records in durable state which compensations it now owes — after reserving stock it owes a release, after charging it owes a refund. When a later step fails, it stops going forward and runs the owed compensations in reverse order, because later steps depend on earlier ones so you unwind in the opposite sequence to how you built up. The orchestrator being the single place that knows the compensation set and their order is precisely why orchestration makes rollback clean, whereas in choreography that logic would be scattered across every service's failure handlers.

Several properties make this safe in production. Compensations must be idempotent, because the orchestrator may retry one after a transient failure and a double refund or double release must be impossible, which I enforce with an idempotency key per compensation. They must be retryable, because a compensation can itself fail, so the orchestrator retries with backoff and alerts for manual intervention if it exhausts its attempts. The orchestrator persists the Saga state so that after a crash it resumes and finishes any pending compensations rather than leaving a half-unwound flow. And I respect non-compensatable steps like physically shipping an item by ordering them last or treating them as pivots after which the Saga can only go forward.

I implemented exactly this for the order Saga at National Bank of India. When shipment scheduling failed after Rajesh's payment had already been charged, a database rollback was useless because the charge had committed in the payment service. The orchestrator, having recorded that stock was reserved and payment charged, drove the rollback in reverse — it cancelled the order, retrying once past a transient failure, then refunded the payment, then released the stock, each compensation idempotent — and marked the Saga cancelled, leaving money refunded, stock released, and nothing shipped. In production I lean on a workflow engine like Temporal or Camunda so the durable Saga state, the automatic retries and timeouts, and the compensation visibility come built in rather than hand-rolled.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: Saga rollback under orchestration is the orchestrator executing idempotent, retryable compensating transactions in reverse order for every step that already committed — refund, release, cancel — because committed local transactions across services cannot be database-rolled-back, and I keep the Saga state durable and use a workflow engine so the rollback is observable, recoverable, and always converges to a consistent cancelled state.
